title: SDN & Network Virtualization
summary: Networks used to be boxes you configured one by one. SDN moves that logic into software. Learn how control plane and data plane split apart, how VXLAN builds virtual networks on shared hardware, and why every cloud provider builds on this.

blocks.markdown:
Every network device does two things: **decide** where traffic goes, and **move** the traffic.

- The **control plane** is the decision layer — routing tables, policy, topology.
- The **data plane** is the forwarding layer — packets in, packets out, as fast as possible.
- Traditionally both live inside each physical device. **SDN** tears them apart — moving the control plane into software.
- **Network virtualization** then lets many logical networks share the same physical hardware.

blocks.subTitle: Key concepts at a glance
blocks.markdown:
The concepts in this topic.

| Concept | One-line meaning |
|---|---|
| Control plane | Computes where packets should go |
| Data plane | Forwards packets at line speed |
| SDN | Moves control plane into centralized software |
| Overlay / VXLAN | Tunnels virtual L2 networks over physical L3 |

blocks.subTitle: Control plane
blocks.markdown:
The **control plane** is the brain of a network device. It decides **where** a packet should go.

- Runs [routing](routing) protocols (OSPF, BGP) to build a map of the network.
- Computes the **routing/forwarding table** that the data plane will use.
- Slow path: runs as software on the device's CPU.
- Changes infrequently — triggered by topology events (link up/down, config change).

blocks.subTitle: Data plane
blocks.markdown:
The **data plane** (also called the **forwarding plane**) actually moves packets.

- Looks up the destination in the forwarding table the control plane built.
- Performs the action: forward out a port, drop, or rewrite headers.
- **Fast path**: implemented in dedicated hardware (ASICs) to handle millions of packets per second.
- Knows nothing about the network map — it just executes the table.

blocks.subTitle: Side by side
blocks.markdown:
The two planes in a single table.

| | Control plane | Data plane |
|---|---|---|
| Job | Compute routes | Forward packets |
| Speed | Slow (CPU) | Fast (ASIC) |
| Changes when | Topology changes | Every packet |
| SDN impact | Lifted out | Stays in hardware |

In traditional networking each switch has its own brain. In SDN one controller programs them all.

RIGHT labelled 'SDN': same 3 switches but brain icons removed from each; a separate box at the top labelled 'SDN Controller' with arrows pointing down to each switch labelled 'flow rules'. - Traditional: each device speaks routing protocols and decides locally.
- SDN: dumb switches forward packets; the controller holds the global view and pushes rules down.

**Software-Defined Networking (SDN)** separates the control plane from the data plane and centralizes it in a software program.

- A single **SDN controller** runs on a server and holds a global view of the network topology.
- Network switches become simple packet-forwarding devices — they ask the controller what to do.
- Changes to routing policy are code changes in the controller, not CLI commands on each box.
- Programmable: plug in an app that adjusts routes based on traffic load, time of day, or security policy.

blocks.subTitle: Controller & southbound APIs
blocks.markdown:
The **SDN controller** communicates with switches via a **southbound API** — the protocol that carries forwarding rules from the controller to the device.

- **OpenFlow** is the first and best-known southbound API. It lets the controller install **flow entries** in a switch's flow table (match on header fields → perform action).
- Other southbound APIs: NETCONF/YANG (config), P4Runtime (programmable dataplanes).
- The controller also exposes a **northbound API** (REST/gRPC) for applications to request network behavior.

blocks.subTitle: Benefits
blocks.markdown:
Why SDN matters.

- **Centralized policy** — one place to define routing, ACLs, QoS. No per-device scripting.
- **Programmability** — network behavior is code; A/B test it, version-control it, automate it.
- **Fast topology response** — controller sees the full graph and can re-route in milliseconds.
- **Vendor independence** — open APIs mean you can mix hardware without vendor lock-in.
- **Foundation for virtual networks** — once you can program the forwarding table, you can carve virtual networks on demand.

**Network virtualization** creates multiple independent logical networks on top of shared physical hardware — the same idea as virtual machines on shared servers.

- Each **virtual network** (tenant or VPC) looks like a private network with its own address space, routing, and isolation.
- Traffic from different virtual networks can share the same physical links without interfering.
- The physical network is called the **underlay**; the logical networks running on top are called **overlays**.
- SDN is what makes this dynamic — rules are pushed by software, so virtual networks can be created, resized, and deleted in seconds.

blocks.subTitle: Overlays and VXLAN
blocks.markdown:
An **overlay** is a virtual network built by tunneling — wrapping one packet inside another to carry it across the physical (underlay) network.

**VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN)** is the dominant overlay protocol:
- **Problem it solves**: VLANs cap virtual networks at 4,096. VXLAN allows ~16 million (24-bit VNI — VXLAN Network Identifier).
- **How it works**: the source host wraps an Ethernet (L2) frame in a UDP packet and sends it over the L3 IP network. The destination host unwraps and delivers.
- L2 semantics (MAC addressing) stretch transparently over an L3 underlay.
- The devices doing the wrapping/unwrapping are called **VTEPs** (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoints) — often the hypervisor's virtual switch.

Every major cloud provider's network is built on these ideas. See [cloud-datacenter-networking](cloud-datacenter-networking).

- A customer's **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** is a network virtualization construct — isolated overlay, private addressing.
- VM-to-VM traffic inside a VPC travels as VXLAN (or a proprietary variant) over the physical fabric.
- Routing rules for each VPC are programmed by an SDN controller at VM spawn time — no human touches a switch.
- Security groups and ACLs are flow rules pushed to the hypervisor's virtual switch (the VTEP), enforced at the source.

Common misconceptions.

- **"SDN replaces the data plane."** No — the data plane still lives in hardware. SDN only moves the control plane into software.
- **"VXLAN eliminates the underlay."** Wrong — VXLAN tunnels ride on top of an IP underlay that must be routed, capacity-planned, and monitored like any network.
- **"The SDN controller is a single point of failure."** It can be — production deployments cluster controllers and add fast failover. Recognize this as an availability concern.
- **"Network virtualization means no IP addressing."** Overlay VMs still have IPs; those IPs are separate from the underlay IPs on the physical NICs.

blocks.subTitle: Control vs data plane
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between the control plane and the data plane?**

The **control plane** decides where packets go — it runs routing protocols, computes tables, and sets policy. The **data plane** executes that decision — it forwards each packet at hardware speed using the table the control plane built. The split exists because decision-making is complex (CPU-level) while forwarding must be simple and extremely fast (ASIC-level).

blocks.subTitle: What is SDN and why
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is SDN and what problem does it solve?**

**SDN (Software-Defined Networking)** lifts the control plane out of each device and centralizes it in a software controller. The problem: traditional networks require per-device CLI configuration — slow, error-prone, impossible to automate at scale. SDN makes the network programmable: policy is code, not config files, and a single controller can reprogram thousands of switches instantly.

blocks.subTitle: Network virtualization
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What problem does network virtualization solve?**

A data center has one physical network but must serve hundreds of tenants, each needing isolation, their own address space, and independent routing. **Network virtualization** creates logical networks on top of shared hardware — each tenant sees a private network, but they all share the same switches and cables. This is how cloud VPCs work.

blocks.subTitle: What is VXLAN
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is VXLAN and why is it used?**

**VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN)** is a tunneling protocol that carries an Ethernet (L2) frame inside a UDP packet across an IP (L3) network. It solves two problems: VLAN's hard limit of 4,096 virtual networks (VXLAN supports ~16 million via a 24-bit VNI), and the need to stretch L2 segments across routed data centers. The hypervisor's virtual switch (VTEP) encapsulates and decapsulates transparently.

blocks.subTitle: OpenFlow's role
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is OpenFlow and where does it fit in SDN?**

**OpenFlow** is a **southbound API** — the protocol a controller uses to install forwarding rules in a switch's flow table. A flow entry says: match packets with these header fields → apply this action (forward, drop, rewrite). OpenFlow was the first open standard that proved controller-switch separation was practical, and it became the reference design for SDN.
